She stresses that this reading is not unanimous: for some the formulations remain ambiguous or hypothetical, Alexander's doctrine unfinished (Frede M., Bobzien), and for D. Frede Alexander and the Stoics amount to two variants of compatibilism. Koch declines to settle this localisation.

scholarly_argument_koch_alexander_s_rhet.description: Koch reports Thillet's political explanation of the De fato's anonymous targets: a book offered to the Emperors, when Septimius Severus wished, like Pertinax, to emulate Marcus Aurelius, could hardly attack Stoic philosophy by name (Thillet 1984; Labarrière 2014). Since anonymity of interlocutors is Alexander's practice elsewhere, she holds that the De fato's particular status can only be one reason among others. Alexander tends not to name contemporaries while naming long-dead philosophers. The dedication to Severus and Antoninus dates the treatise between 198 and 209.

scholarly_argument_koch_alexander_s_targ.description: Koch reports, without endorsing, the verdict of Gercke, Long, Duhot and Inwood that Alexander attacks 'une doctrine reconstruite et simplifiée', an adversary made to measure, with distortions that seem deliberate. Against reading the De fato's doctrinal peculiarities as clumsy or malicious deformations, she proposes a richer alternative: Alexander's anonymous interlocutors are imperial-era Stoics faithful to a Chrysippean orthodoxy whose formulations had evolved after five centuries of inter-school competition — while granting that Stoic determinism is beyond doubt the treatise's principal target.

scholarly_argument_denzey_lewis_astral_d.description: The Gospel of Judas invokes the language of astral fatalism frequently, but its discourse of astral enslavement nowhere draws on contemporaneous Graeco-Roman cosmology or philosophical physics; its author draws on older Jewish apocalyptic traditions equating the stars with the priests administering the Jerusalem Temple. The word heimarmene and the concept of Pronoia are absent, and the text — unlike the others discussed in the book — offers no system of salvation or 'way out'. Yet its rhetorical deployment of sidereal enslavement is identical with other second- and third-century texts.

Second-century Christians, 'Gnostic' and 'proto-orthodox' alike, agreed that baptism had resounding cosmological ramifications: they were 'enslaved to fate' only until baptism.

scholarly_argument_denzey_lewis_heimarme.description: Heimarmene is mentioned in only six of the fifty-two Nag Hammadi tractates: the Hermetic Discourse on the Eighth and Ninth; Eugnostos and the Sophia of Jesus Christ, which explicitly reject it as a source of being or influence; and the Trimorphic Protennoia, Apocryphon of John and On the Origin of the World, which adopt it as a causal principle within the cosmic oikonomia while disagreeing on its effects and consequences (ch. 4). The Gospel of Judas (Codex Tchacos) lacks the word altogether, as it lacks Pronoia (p. 165).

scholarly_argument_denzey_lewis_middle_p.description: In the period when the Hermetic writings were composed, the Middle Platonists who chiefly inspired the Hermetists had moved away from the more integrative Stoic conception of heimarmene as a universal principle working through all things: it was theoretically possible to stand outside its influence. Hermetists, like Middle Platonists, actively debated how to delineate heimarmene from necessity and providence — partly to save divine providence from misfortune and evil, attributable to the lesser principle of fate; some Hermetic texts identified heimarmene with specific celestial bodies (planetary, astral or zodiacal).

scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_co.description: As reported by the reviewer P. M. Huby adds that 'his central theme is not entirely clear' and herself objects that 'it is unlikely that Aristotle held a consistent and plausible theory'. The fonds holds only Huby's review and the 2010 English translation (chs. I-V), not Donini's own statement of this thesis.

evidence.quote: Because he - rightly - discusses much on the level of detail, his central theme is not entirely clear, but he seems to believe that Aristotle held a consistent theory, or set of theories, about these matters throughout his life.
in general consistent theories are implausible, and plausible ones inconsistent upon close examination. Hence it is unlikely that Aristotle held a consistent and plausible theory.

scholarly_argument_donini_aristotle_s_co.finding: The claim rests on Huby's review, not on Donini's own words. Huby hedges ('his central theme is not entirely clear, but he seems to believe…') and immediately objects that a consistent and plausible theory is 'unlikely'. The node states the thesis flatly as Donini's and drops both the hedge and the reviewer's dissent. Printed p. 370 is legible in the file (running head '370 THE CLASSICAL REVIEW', line 14) but agentic_search refuses the file (AUDIT-INSUFFICIENT_SAMPLES, map_conf 0.50, page_map gives 'p.1'), so page left empty. scholarly_argument_donini_nicomachean_et.description: Donini (Ethos ch. V; Engl. tr. 2010, pp. 103-105) finds that NE III 5, 1113b7-14, where agents 'always have two possible options', 'seems utterly incompatible with the theory of unidirectionality of habits'. Rather than leaving the inconsistency, he offers two reconciling hypotheses (the original indeterminacy of the not-yet-formed character; a habit is not 'an absolutely irreversible condition'), concluding that 'it is legitimate for Aristotle to say that everyone has the option of doing good or evil even after the acquisition of a habit'. Huby (CR 1991, pp. 370-371) objects that Aristotle here merely shows virtue and vice are voluntary and that Donini's psychological qualifications are 'misplaced'.

evidence.quote: It would be inappropriate at this point to add qualifications about human psychology such as D. wants. So his claim that this passage is inconsistent with the view found elsewhere that a virtuous man can act only virtuously is misplaced.
Aristotle could coherently state in NE that every agent has the option of deciding in favor of a bad or a virtuous action if this thesis meant something different in NE than it seems to do in EE.
evidence.citation: [Pier Luigi Donini - Aristotle and Determinism (2010, Peeters) - libgen.li.md:4123-4125]

evidence.quote: but he could still lose that habit, so it is legitimate for Aristotle to say that everyone has the option of doing good or evil even after the acquisition of a habit that, in fact, constrains them to always decide in one way and one direction only.

scholarly_argument_donini_nicomachean_et.finding: Two problems. V 'Character and indeterminacy', pp. 103-105) does not simply 'argue that this passage is inconsistent': he says NE III 5, 1113b7-14 'seems utterly incompatible with the theory of unidirectionality of habits' and then proposes two hypotheses to reconcile them, concluding that 'it is legitimate for Aristotle to say that everyone has the option of doing good or evil even after the acquisition of a habit'. scholarly_argument_engberg_pedersen_dete.description: Engberg-Pedersen presents the I→X→S model as 'the basic logical shape' of Paul's and of Stoic 'anthropology' and 'ethics' (p. 33), and insists that Stoic ethics be studied 'as a comprehensive philosophical system', 'not just … individual motifs' such as the sophos, the adiaphora or Stoic 'freedom' (eleutheria) that 'most scholars have heard of' (p. 45). These pages say nothing about determinism or fate, nor describe freedom and the sage as 'structured human agency within a cosmic order'; the fonds extraction contains only chapter-opening pages, so no such claim is verifiable.

evidence.quote: The model pertains most directly to Paul's 'anthropology' and 'ethics'. It expresses the basic logical shape of that- as well as of Stoic 'anthropology' and 'ethics'.

Most scholars have heard of, say, the Stoic wise man (sophos), the 'in- differents' (adiaphora) or Stoic 'freedom' (eleutheria), but few have studied Stoic ethics as a comprehensive philosophical system.
We want to obtain a sure grasp of Stoic ethics as a whole, not just to look at individual motifs.

scholarly_argument_engberg_pedersen_dete.finding: The first two clauses are supported (p. 33: model = 'basic logical shape' of Pauline and Stoic 'anthropology' and 'ethics'; p. 45: Stoic ethics to be studied 'as a comprehensive philosophical system', not 'individual motifs'). The last clause (freedom and the sage 'not reducible to simple determinism but involve structured human agency within a cosmic order') is nowhere on these pages: p. 45 merely lists sophos, adiaphora and eleutheria as motifs scholars 'have heard of'. Neither determinism nor fate is discussed. The fonds file is a partial extraction (first page of each chapter only), so the claim cannot be checked elsewhere. No page_map; printed pages read from footers (33 at line 121, 45 at line 160); page left empty.

scholarly_argument_engberg_pedersen_free.description: Engberg-Pedersen's I→X→S model (p. 33) is a 'heuristic' abstraction stating 'the basic logical shape' of Pauline and Stoic 'anthropology' and 'ethics', 'identical with neither' but including 'an extensive area of overlap'. The X-pole is the normative point 'with which one identifies oneself, one for which Christ, as it were, stands' (p. 105). The extracted pages contain no contrast with 'libertarian free will' or 'pure determinism' and no 'teleological framework'; those are the node's terms, not the author's.

evidence.quote: It is an abstraction, drawn from the particularities of Paul's thought in three of his letters and from Stoicism in the many forms in which we know it. It is identical with neither. It leaves something out of both bodies of thought, while focusing attention on other things. But it also includes an extensive area of overlap between Stoic and Pauline 'anthropology' and 'ethics'.

It is also a matter of acquiring a new form of propositional know- ledge: a piece of normative knowledge that defines the X-pole with which one identifies oneself, one for which Christ, as it were, stands.

scholarly_argument_engberg_pedersen_free.finding: The core (I→X→S model shared by Paul and Stoics; X-pole = the normative point with which the I identifies, 'for which Christ, as it were, stands') is attested, but the identification of the X-pole is on p. 105 (ch. 5), not on the listed pages. The contrast 'rather than radical libertarian free will or pure determinism' and the 'teleological framework' appear nowhere in the extracted pages; 'libertarian' is imported vocabulary the author does not use here. The S-pole ('new social togetherness') is not described on any extracted page. No page_map; page left empty (footers: 33 at line 121, 105 at line 234).

scholarly_argument_koch_aristotle_s_alle.description: Koch (pp. 36-37) stresses Alexander's 'travail de construction' undertaken 'sur la base d'un donné aristotélicien quasi inexistant'. Facing the De fato's announced aim of expounding Aristotle's doctrine on fate, modern readers and translators 'ont tous souligné' that Aristotle elaborated no doctrine of fate and that the term εἱμαρμένη occurs nowhere in his transmitted writings, except once in the Poetics, where 'le terme n'y est pas employé pour lui-même par Aristote': it comes from his summary of an episode of the lost tragedy Phineidai.

evidence.quote: Le premier point que je développerai ici touche précisément à ce travail de construction, qu’Alexandre entreprend sur la base d’un donné aristotélicien quasi inexistant et dans un contexte scolaire jusqu’à lui peu développé.

les lecteurs et traducteurs modernes du traité ont tous souligné que non seulement Aristote n’avait élaboré aucune doctrine du destin, mais qu’on ne pouvait même relever aucun emploi du terme εἱμαρμένη dans tous ses écrits transmis.

Une unique occurrence s’en trouve dans la Poétique, mais le terme n’y est pas employé pour lui‑même par Aristote : il s’agit d’un passage où Aristote résume un épisode dramatique des Phinéides, tragédie que nous ne connaissons que par cette citation

scholarly_argument_koch_aristotle_s_alle.finding: Quote verbatim at p. 36 (conf 0.95). Two qualifications lost: (1) Koch attributes the observation that Aristotle elaborated no doctrine of fate and never uses the term to 'les lecteurs et traducteurs modernes du traité' who 'ont tous souligné' it — a reported consensus, not her own discovery; (2) the single Poetics occurrence is characterised not as 'non-technical meaning' but as 'pas employé pour lui-même par Aristote': it belongs to Aristotle's summary of a tragic plot (the lost Phineidai), pp. 36-37. The constructive-project point is faithful.

scholarly_argument_koch_chronological_an.description: Koch (p. 34): the formal and doctrinal resemblances between the De fato and the writings on providence are such that 'il est … difficile de proposer une hypothèse sur la chronologie des deux traités'. Her reading hypothesis: 'le traité Sur le destin vient préciser et compléter certains thèmes abordés dans les écrits sur la providence qui n'en proposaient pas un traitement totalement satisfaisant'.

evidence.quote: Les ressemblances, formelles et doctrinales, sont telles qu’il est d’ailleurs difficile de proposer une hypothèse sur la chronologie des deux traités 4.
Il me semble que le traité Sur le destin vient préciser et compléter certains thèmes abordés dans les écrits sur la providence qui n’en proposaient pas un traitement totalement satisfaisant.

scholarly_argument_koch_chronological_an.finding: Description faithful (similarities make chronology hard; De fato 'vient préciser et compléter' themes of the writings on providence). But the passage is on printed p. 34 (page_map conf 0.95: line 72 → p. 34; running head '34 ISABELLE KOCH' at line 50, next head p. 35 at line 96), not p. 35.

scholarly_argument_koch_middle_platonic_.description: Koch (p. 35): the Platonists 'ont actualisé leur platonisme' by rereading founding texts to develop 'la théorie originale du destin conditionnel', found in Alcinous Did. 26, Calcidius In Tim. 142-144, Nemesius Nat. hom. 38 and ps.-Plutarch De fato; she sums it up (n. 7): our actions are free, but once done their consequences are 'soumises au destin et inévitables'. The suggestion that Alexander probably knew this theory but omitted it 'pour ne pas faire de publicité à une école rivale' is Sharples's (On Fate, p. 14), reported by Koch in n. 8 (p. 36).

evidence.quote: C’est ainsi que les Platoniciens, sur les questions du destin et de la providence, ont actualisé leur platonisme en opérant une relecture de quelques textes fondateurs5 pour développer la théorie originale du destin conditionnel6
On peut résumer cette doctrine du destin conditionné comme suit : nos actions sont libres, mais, une fois que nous avons agi, les conséquences de nos actions sont soumises au destin et inévitables

Selon Sharples, Alexandre connaissait vraisemblablement la théorie médioplato‑ nicienne du destin conditionnel, mais il n’y fait aucune allusion dans son De fato, peut‑être pour ne pas faire de publicité à une école rivale dans un livre célébrant son accès à la tête de l’école aristotélicienne (On Fate, op. cit., p. 14).

scholarly_argument_koch_middle_platonic_.finding: The first half is Koch's (p. 35 and n. 7 for the summary 'nos actions sont libres, mais … les conséquences … sont soumises au destin et inévitables'). The second half — Alexander probably knew the theory but omitted it so as not to advertise a rival school in a book celebrating his accession — is Sharples's hypothesis (On Fate, p. 14), explicitly introduced by 'Selon Sharples' in n. 8 (p. 36). The node presents it as Koch's own position.

scholarly_argument_koch_peripatetic_defi.description: Koch (p. 34) holds that the Peripatetic definitions of providence and of fate in the two treatises 'sont très proches et cherchent visiblement à répondre à des préoccupations identiques', so close 'qu'on pourrait se demander en quoi les deux concepts diffèrent'. The observation that Alexander's restriction of fate 'à la sphère du τέλος qui doit être poursuivi par les causes efficientes, antécédentes et naturelles' brings his conception of fate 'grandement' close to providence is Jaap Mansfeld's ('Diaphonia', Phronesis 33, 1988, p. 195), quoted by Koch (n. 3).

evidence.quote: la définition péripatéticienne de la providence et celle du destin dans l’un et l’autre traités sont très proches et cherchent visiblement à répondre à des préoccupations identiques. La proximité est même si grande qu’on pourrait se demander en quoi les deux concepts diffèrent, comme le note Jaap Mansfeld :

On pourrait souligner que la restriction, opérée par Alexandre, de la portée du destin (dans le De fato) à la sphère du τέλος qui doit être poursuivi par les causes efficientes, antécédentes et naturelles, rapproche grandement sa conception du destin du concept de providence.3
3. Ibid., p. 195 : «So Alexander at least tried to keep the twins apart, although, as we shall see, there is some inevitable overlapping.

scholarly_argument_koch_peripatetic_defi.finding: The first clause is Koch's (p. 34; also abstract p. 33). The second clause — Alexander restricts fate to the sphere of the τέλος pursued by efficient, antecedent, natural causes, bringing fate close to providence — is a quotation from Jaap Mansfeld ('Diaphonia', Phronesis 33, 1988, p. 195), translated by Koch and introduced by 'comme le note Jaap Mansfeld' (n. 3 gives the English original). The node attributes Mansfeld's observation to Koch.

scholarly_argument_pr_aux_fate_and_free_.description: Préaux (pp. 395-398) reconsiders an aspect 'jusqu'ici curieusement négligé' of the Octavius: the argument drawn from 'la doctrine du fatalisme philosophique' advanced by the pagan Caecilius (XI, 5-6) and Octavius' refutation (XXXVI, 1-2), set within the apologist's mainly philosophical demonstration of divine providence. He finds it surprising that the sources of these passages have hardly been sought, and insists that the apologist 'n'a pas tiré de son fonds' the answers he merely sketches ('esquisse'). His thesis is that the treatment is borrowed, not that it is sophisticated.

evidence.quote: Il s'agit de l'argument emprunté à la doctrine du fatalisme philosophique qu'avance le païen Caecilius au chapi- tre xi, 5-6, et de la réfutation que lui apporte le chrétien Octavius au chapitre xxxvi, 1-2.

Il est étonnant que l'on n'ait guère recherché, à ma connais- sance, les sources de la pensée de Minucius Felix dans ces passages importants qui traitent un problème situé au cœur même de la théologie et de la philosophie. Il est clair, cependant, que l'apolo- giste habile n'a pas tiré de son fonds les données et les réponses qu'il esquisse

scholarly_argument_pr_aux_fate_and_free_.finding: Quote verbatim (lines 42-49, printed p. 395). But what Préaux calls 'curieusement négligé' is a specific argument (Caecilius' fatalist argument, Oct. XI, 5-6, and Octavius' refutation, XXXVI, 1-2) and, on p. 398, the search for its sources — not a 'sophisticated philosophical treatment'. Préaux stresses the opposite: the apologist 'n'a pas tiré de son fonds' his answers, which he only 'esquisse', and Octavius himself calls it brief ('Ac de fato satis, uel si pauca pro tempore'). 'Determinism' is not Préaux's word (he writes fatum, 'fatalisme philosophique'). No page_map; pages 395-398 from running heads; page left empty.

scholarly_argument_pr_aux_interpretation.description: In his translation of Oct. XXXVI, 2 Préaux renders genitura as 'thème de géniture' and notes (p. 397 n. 2) that it is 'rapproché intentionnellement de ingenii natura pour former un jeu de mots, lourd de sens'. In the discussion (pp. 410-411) he explains that genitura designated either a birth horoscope in astrological language or, more generally, 'la nature engendrée, la créature', and that here 'tous les deux conviennent': whichever sense is taken, what is punished is neither the horoscope nor created nature but the ingenii natura — a doctrine he traces to Origen.

evidence.quote: (2) C'est le sens que j'adopte pour genitura rapproché intentionnellement
de ingenii natura pour former un jeu de mots, lourd de sens si on le replace dans la pensée de Minucius Felix. Voir plus loin la discussion, pp. 410-411.

Quel que soit le sens qu'on donne à ce terme technique dans ce contexte-ci - et tous les deux con- viennent - , ce n'est ni le thème de géniture ni la nature créée qui est l'objet d'un châtiment divin, mais bien, affirme Octavius, Yingenii natura

scholarly_argument_pr_aux_interpretation.finding: Préaux does translate genitura as 'thème de géniture' and speaks of an intentional 'jeu de mots' with ingenii natura (p. 397 n. 2, continued p. 398, lines 193, 241-242). But in the announced discussion (pp. 410-411, lines 872-896) he allows both senses of genitura — horoscope in astrological language, or 'la nature engendrée, la créature' — and says 'tous les deux conviennent'; the point of the wordplay is that punishment falls on the ingenii natura, read through Origen's thought. The node drops this qualification. The Greek equivalent given in the file is OCR-corrupt ('( yévsaiç )', line 873) and cannot be verified. No page_map; page left empty.

scholarly_argument_pr_aux_minucius_felix.description: Préaux (p. 398) holds it 'impossible d'admettre que Minucius Felix ait fait preuve d'originalité' on the fatum/providence problem: his characteristic way of resolving it 'lui a été inspirée par la démonstration d'un docteur de l'Église'. Since before Augustine no Latin Doctor treated the problem (Tertullian silent, Cyprian likewise; Arnobius and Lactantius merely touch it, p. 399), the source is Greek: the 'procédé d'exposition a été emprunté, à mon sens, à Origène' (p. 401), whose exegesis of Rom 9 Caecilius' argument 'imite à la lettre' (p. 402).

evidence.quote: lui a été inspirée par la démonstration d'un docteur de l'Église. Il est impossible d'admettre que Minucius Felix ait fait preuve d'originalité sur ce point aussi capital que délicat à traiter.
Avant saint Augustin, personne parmi les Docteurs de l'Église, écrivant en latin, n'a traité ce

Ce procédé d'exposition a été emprunté, à mon sens, à Origène et c'est à la lumière des démonstrations célèbres que le grand penseur d'Alexandrie a fournies entre 220 et 250 que se révèlent les sources de la pensée de l'avocat romain

scholarly_argument_pr_aux_minucius_felix.finding: Quote verbatim (lines 219-228, printed p. 398). Two qualifications lost: Préaux speaks of 'la démonstration d'un docteur de l'Église' (singular), and the point about Latin writers is not that the source is 'difficult to identify' but that no Latin Doctor before Augustine treated the problem at all (Tertullian, Cyprian silent; Arnobius and Lactantius only touch it, p. 399), so that the source must be Greek — which he identifies as Origen (p. 401: 'Ce procédé d'exposition a été emprunté, à mon sens, à Origène'; p. 402: Caecilius 'imite à la lettre l'exégèse origéniste'). No page_map; pages from running heads; page left empty.

scholarly_argument_sorabji_epictetus_on_.description: For Sorabji (pp. 49-50) Epictetus' eleutheria is 'a genuine freedom, but rare': through 'careful adjudication of desires' one is 'enslaved to nothing', and the resulting 'rare kind of invulnerability' is why the person is called free. Epictetus regards this freedom as compatible with compulsion and with Stoic determinism. Against Frede, Sorabji does not present it as an incomplete free will but as a freedom 'very different' from the voluntas libera of Lucretius and Cicero and from Christian free will (p. 63), even though Justin, Tatian and Origen borrowed Epictetus' terminology for 'a completely different idea of freedom' (p. 64).

evidence.quote: Stoic freedom is only one of the positive types, but Berlin in his lecture classed it as sour grapes rather than freedom: we don’t want what we can’t get.2 I think it was a genuine freedom, but rare.
evidence.citation: [Seaford, Richard_ Wilkins, John_ Wright, Matthew Ephraim (eds.) - Selfhood and the soul _ essays on ancient thought and literature in honour of Christopher Gill-Oxford University Press (2017).md:2135-2138]

evidence.quote: Not only does Epictetus regard this freedom as compatible with compulsion; he views it as so obviously compatible with the Stoic belief in determinism, that is, with the idea that whatever happens has all along been necessary or inevitable,4 that he does not even mention deterministic necessity throughout his discourse on freedom.
evidence.citation: [Seaford, Richard_ Wilkins, John_ Wright, Matthew Ephraim (eds.) - Selfhood and the soul _ essays on ancient thought and literature in honour of Christopher Gill-Oxford University Press (2017).md:2161-2166]

evidence.quote: (iii) It is true that Epictetus does have the idea of prohairesis being free, but this important, but rarely achieved freedom, is compatible with things having all along been inevitable and with every attempt at duress. It is very different from the freedom of voluntas invoked before Epictetus by Lucretius and Cicero

More importantly, 'not yet the full concept of free will' is not his framing: against Frede he treats Epictetus' free prohairesis as a different freedom, 'very different' from the voluntas libera of Lucretius/Cicero and from Christian free will (p. 63), while granting that Justin, Tatian and Origen borrowed the terminology for 'a completely different idea of freedom' (p. 64). scholarly_argument_sorabji_freedom_and_t.description: Sorabji distinguishes four strands in the idea of will — rationality, freedom, will power, will perverted by pride — each arising separately (Plato, Aristotle, Posidonius, Lucretius, Plotinus) and 'first (in Augustine) all assembled'; hence 'it may be better not to ask who discovered the will' (pp. 54-58). Against Frede he is 'not persuaded about Epictetus having anticipated later concepts of will' (four hesitations, pp. 62-63) and finds Epictetus' account of free will 'very unlike' Augustine's (p. 59), while acknowledging that Justin, Tatian and Origen borrowed Epictetus' terminology to express 'a completely different idea of freedom' (p. 64).

evidence.quote: Because each of these strands in the idea of will had arisen separately before Augustine, I concluded in my earlier treatment that it may be better not to ask who discovered the will, but rather to trace the different contexts in which the various components were thought up, and when they were ﬁrst (in Augustine) all assembled.44

On will: the four strands arose separately (Plato, Aristotle, Posidonius, Lucretius, Plotinus) and were 'ﬁrst (in Augustine) all assembled', so 'it may be better not to ask who discovered the will'; against Frede he is 'not persuaded about Epictetus having anticipated later concepts of will' (four hesitations, pp. 62-63). scholarly_argument_sorabji_lucretius_on_.description: Sorabji (pp. 52-53): Lucretius 'bases freedom on a swerve of the atoms'; voluntas 'is not an agent in its own right, but a capacity or act of animus', the central part, seated in the heart, of the physical soul anima. Sorabji hesitates to translate voluntas as 'will', since 'it is not a rational enough desire' (it is found in horses), and stresses that Lucretius opposes free willing 'not to necessitation itself, but to a Fate or Fates … that operate from indefinitely far back'; the appeal to necessity from infinite time 'reflects the rise of the opposing Stoic view that things have indeed been fated for the whole of time'.

evidence.quote: I hesitate to translate voluntas as ‘will’ not for this reason, but because it is not a rational enough desire, since it is found in horses (2. 261–93). He opposes free willing not to necessitation itself, but to a Fate or Fates (fatum, fata) that operate from indeﬁnitely far back

scholarly_argument_amand_de_mendieta_ast.description: Amand: throughout Greek and Christian antiquity astrology was 'essentiellement et radicalement fataliste'; the theory of heimarmene and that of 'universal sympathy' formed its doctrinal basis, and absolute fatalism was a postulate taught and admitted by all astrologers. Consequently almost all ('presque toutes') the attacks on astrology by Hellenic philosophers and Christian theologians were in reality aimed at the fatalism bound up with the science of the 'Chaldeans'. He stresses that his work is purely historical and no war-machine against astrology itself.

scholarly_argument_amand_de_mendieta_car.description: Amand: the moral argumentation drawn from the disastrous moral consequences of the doctrine of heimarmene is the one Carneades 'sinon inventée, du moins aiguisée et popularisée' against Stoic dogmatism; the book studies its survival among later Greek philosophers and Greek Christian theologians of the first four centuries. Six 'textes témoins' (Philo, Alexander, Firmicus Maternus, Eusebius, Chrysostom, ps-Chrysostom), plus Bardesane, Basil, the Arian commentator on Job and Nemesius, ground a conjectural reconstruction by synoptic comparison ('règle de fer': Carneadean if attested by 3 of 6). Amand proposes no linear chain of transmission between the witnesses.

scholarly_argument_amand_de_mendieta_met.description: Amand never intended to write a history of the anti-fatalist polemic; the title 'Fatalisme et liberté' should not mislead readers seeking a synthetic, philosophically conceived exposition. His 'méthode strictement philologique et historique' obliged him to present a primarily documentary study and to stay behind texts clear enough by themselves; the same historical method led him to set the philosophers and Christian doctors in their concrete intellectual milieu, sketch their personality, note the Christians' attitude to Hellenic philosophy and how each conceived 'la liberté du vouloir'.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_free_will_a.description: Dettwiler on the parenesis (4,1-6,9): its foundation (4,1-16) puts all the emphasis on the unity of the Church, formulated as a liturgical acclamation (4,4-6); 4,17-24 is a general exhortation stressing the necessary distancing from pagan life and clarifying the Church's relation to the surrounding world; 4,25-5,20 resists structuring, its exhortations becoming more concrete and associative; 5,21-6,9 is the household code. Nothing is said about free will, moral responsibility or individual moral autonomy.

evidence.quote: Le fondement de la parénèse en Ép 4,1-16 met tout l'accent sur l'unité de l'Église, que l'auteur formule dans le style de l'acclama- tion liturgique (4,4-6)

4,17-24 est une exhortation générale, qui met l'accent sur la nécessaire mise à distance de la vie païenne et clarifie ainsi le rapport de l'Église avec le monde ambiant; la partie suivante (4,25-5,20) résiste à une structuration pertinente; les exhortations deviennent plus concrètes

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_theological.description: Dettwiler: Ephesians is characterised above all by a deepened reflection on the nature and task of the one, universal Church, a theological reflection without comparison in the canon. Col and Eph form the backbone of the 'école paulinienne'. The 'sketch (Col) to fully achieved realisation (Eph)' formula, Eph being more coherent and systematic, is cited as one way exegetes have defined the relation ('On a défini par exemple'); Dettwiler's own conclusion ('Quoi qu'il en soit') is that Eph drew heavily on its 'sœur aînée' while pursuing a specific theological line.

evidence.quote: On a défini par exemple leur relation comme la transition d'une esquisse (Col) à une réalisa- tion pleinement achevée (Ép), en soulignant que la dernière serait théologique- ment plus cohérente et plus systématique que la première. Quoi qu'il en soit, il semble clair qu 'Ép s'est fortement inspirée de sa «sœur aînée»

Cette épître se caractérise avant tout par une réflexion approfondie sur la nature et la tâche de l'Église une et univer- selle; cette réflexion théologique ne connaît pas de comparaison dans le canon

scholarly_argument_djeranian_chrysippus_.description: D'Jeranian: as reported by Cicero (De fato 41-43), Chrysippus's strategy (cylinder analogy; fate as antecedent and auxiliary cause, assent as principal cause) guarantees 'a minima' man's causal autonomy within the determined world, yet seems to contradict the subjection of assent to fate; since assent cannot be both autonomous and fated, Chrysippean 'compatibilisme' 'aboutirait finalement à un échec'. That the strategy succeeds only against the anti-fatalist objection but not in grounding moral responsibility is Salles's conclusion (2005), followed by Gourinat, which D'Jeranian reports in a note.

evidence.quote: Ainsi rapportée, la stratégie de Chrysippe garantit a minima l’autonomie causale de l’homme au sein du monde déterminé, mais semble malgré tout contredire, par la rupture qu’elle implique dans la séquence causale représentation-assentiment, la soumission de l’assentiment au destin.

R. Salles (2005, p. 47-49) conclut que la stratégie de Chrysippe réussit dans le cadre de l’objection anti-fataliste uniquement (mais pas pour fonder la responsabilité morale). Opinion suivie par Gourinat 2005, p. 272-273.
Mais elles obtinrent des résultats en demi-teinte, et ne légitimèrent plus tant la responsabilité morale que l’autonomie causale de l’homme dans l’économie du destin

scholarly_argument_djeranian_chrysippus_.finding: Quote_verbatim located verbatim at l. 266-270, p. 5 of the author's version (agentic_search: p.5, map_conf 0.95; the file is a 17-page author manuscript, not the journal pagination). First clause is D'Jeranian's, but in the conditional ('aboutirait finalement à un échec') and as the outcome of Cicero's critique. The second clause — 'succeeds only against the anti-fatalist objection but not for grounding moral responsibility properly speaking' — is Salles's conclusion (2005, pp. 47-49), 'suivie par Gourinat', reported in n. 12 (l. 123-124); D'Jeranian's own formulation is that the strategy guarantees 'a minima l'autonomie causale de l'homme'. Page range 1-2 should be 2, 5.

scholarly_argument_djeranian_cicero_s_cr.description: D'Jeranian's reading of Cicero: the strategy does not satisfy Cicero, who judges that legitimate moral and juridical evaluations require that assent not be the effect of antecedent external causes. Chrysippus, convinced of the freedom of the soul's movements (Fat. 39), should have said so explicitly, at the risk otherwise of confirming the necessitarian position; the break introduced in the representation-assent sequence would thus force him to join the anti-fatalist camp by explicitly withdrawing assent from fate (Fat. 44). Assent cannot be both autonomous and determined, since the preceding representation cannot be both cause and condition of its autonomous movement (Fat. 34-36).

evidence.quote: Toutefois, cette stratégie ne satisfait pas Cicéron, qui juge que l’autonomie de l’individu, pour que les évaluations morales et juridiques puissent être légitimes, exige que l’assentiment ne soit pas l’effet de causes externes antécédentes.
C’est d’ailleurs ce que Chrysippe, convaincu de la liberté des mouvements de l’âme (Fat. 39), aurait dû explicitement dire au risque de confirmer la position nécessitariste.

contraindrait donc Chrysippe à rallier le camp des anti-fatalistes en soustrayant explicitement l’assentiment au destin (Fat. 44). L’assentiment ne pourra donc être à la fois autonome et déterminé, parce que la représentation qui le précède ne peut en être à la fois la cause et la condition de son mouvement autonome (Fat. 34-36).

scholarly_argument_djeranian_cicero_s_cr.finding: Quote_verbatim located verbatim (l. 81-91), p. 2 of the author's version. The description overstates and muddles: D'Jeranian writes that the strategy 'ne satisfait pas Cicéron, qui juge que...' and uses the conditional throughout ('aurait dû', 'contraindrait'), not 'Cicero demonstrates'. The clause 'abandoning his fatalist position and confirming (despite himself) the necessity of fate' contradicts the text: the dilemma is that Chrysippus should have explicitly withdrawn assent from external antecedent causes (joining the anti-fatalists, Fat. 44) 'au risque de confirmer la position nécessitariste' otherwise; there is no 'confirms the necessity of fate'.

scholarly_argument_djeranian_the_cylinde.description: D'Jeranian: in De fato 42-43 Chrysippus's manoeuvre dissociates the necessity of fate and preserves the individual's autonomy by making fate the antecedent and auxiliary cause of his action; man's movement is like a cylinder reacting to an external push in a way determined by the 'nature et force propre' of its principal cause — which is assent itself, not the ruling part of the soul. On Cicero's critique, the break this introduces in the representation-assent sequence, conceived to 'fuir la nécessité' and legitimise moral evaluations, would ('contraindrait') force Chrysippus into the anti-fatalist camp by withdrawing assent from fate (Fat. 44).

evidence.quote: Dans le De fato (§§42-43), cette manœuvre dissocie la nécessité du destin et préserve l’autonomie de l’individu, en faisant du destin la cause antécédente et auxiliaire de l’action de ce dernier.
seulement que c’est l’assentiment, et non la partie directrice de l’âme, qui agit selon sa force et sa nature

scholarly_argument_djeranian_the_cylinde.finding: Quote_verbatim located verbatim (l. 77-80), p. 2 of the author's version. Two qualifications lost: (1) the 'nature et force propre' belongs to the principal cause, which D'Jeranian identifies with assent itself, 'et non la partie directrice de l'âme' (p. 5, l. 256-257) — not 'the individual's nature and force'; (2) 'forces Chrysippus to join the anti-fatalist camp' is the upshot of Cicero's critique stated in the conditional ('contraindrait'), not a flat outcome.

scholarly_argument_koch_academic_reactio.description: Koch: the Academic reactions to Chrysippus's causal distinctions, traces of which Cicero's De fato preserves, met the distinctions with 'de très fortes résistances'; she studies them in section II and then links these Stoic/Neo-Academic discussions to Plato's contrasting positions on the proper and improper uses of the term cause, which she thinks form a sub-text of the debates Cicero stages.

evidence.quote: J’en viendrai ensuite à l’étude des réactions académiciennes à ces distinctions, réactions dont on trouve trace également dans le De fato de Cicéron (II).
Or, les distinctions appliquées par Chrysippe à l’analyse de la causalité physique, dans le cadre de sa défense de la doctrine du destin, ont suscité de très fortes résistances.

scholarly_argument_koch_academic_reactio.finding: Quote_verbatim located verbatim (l. 167-172) on printed p. 90 (header '90 ISABELLE KOCH' at l. 143; '91' at l. 187), not p. 91; page_range '91' and quote_page '90' are inconsistent. Section II 'Les critiques académiciennes' begins at l. 807, p. 104 (headers 103 at l. 737, 105 at l. 830), and runs to p. 115. Description otherwise fair; 'significant philosophical engagement' is a gloss on Koch's 'de très fortes résistances'.

scholarly_argument_koch_platonic_backgro.description: Koch: Carneades' critique of Chrysippus in De fato 34-36, which sets his doctrine of antecedent causes against the canonical Stoic definition of cause, probably rests on an earlier discussion, prior to the Stoa and going back to the Old Academy, about what may legitimately be called a cause; Plato (Phaedo 99b; Timaeus 46c-e) offers the first exclusive handling of the notion of cause and a strict delimitation of proper and improper uses of the term, which she takes to form a sub-text of the debates Cicero stages.

evidence.quote: Il est probable que la critique que Carnéade adresse à Chrysippe en De fato 34‑36, mettant en conflit sa doctrine des causes antécédentes avec la définition stoïcienne canonique de la cause, s’appuie sur une première discussion, antérieure au Portique et remontant à l’Ancienne Académie
positions dont on peut penser qu’elles forment un sous‑texte des débats que met en scène Cicéron (III).

scholarly_argument_koch_platonic_backgro.finding: Quote_verbatim located verbatim (l. 1343-1349), printed p. 116 (agentic_search: p.116, map_conf 0.98; headers 115 at l. 1287, 117 at l. 1378); the programme statement is p. 90 (l. 169-172). Page range '91' is wrong. Description faithful. The verified_reference's 'Phaedo 99a-b, Timaeus 28a' does not match Koch's citations: she cites Phédon 99b 2-6 (n. 85, l. 1376) and Timée 46c 7-e7 (n. 93, l. 1463).

scholarly_argument_koch_stoic_causal_the.description: Koch: Cicero's De fato is valuable because it attributes precise causal distinctions unambiguously to Chrysippus and indicates their context, which confirms that these distinctions become useful, and are then drawn, within the problematic of responsibility: when it is a question of grounding human responsibility, either against the determinism attributed to the Stoics (the position given to Carneades in the treatise) or inside the doctrine that everything happens by fate (Chrysippus's own position). Chrysippus's distinctions (causae perfectae et principales vs adiuvantes et proximae, De fato 41) thus serve to ground responsibility within fate, not against determinism.

evidence.quote: elles apparaissent lorsqu’il est question de fonder la responsabilité humaine, qu’il s’agisse de la fonder contre le déterminisme attribué aux Stoïciens (position notamment attribuée à Carnéade dans le traité) ou de la fonder à l’intérieur de la doctrine selon laquelle tout arrive par le destin (position défendue par Chrysippe).
D’où l’intérêt du De fato de Cicéron, qui attribue sans ambiguïté des distinctions causales précises à Chrysippe, en indiquant en outre le contexte de leur formulation.

scholarly_argument_koch_stoic_causal_the.finding: Quote_verbatim located verbatim (l. 157-166), printed p. 90. The description inverts Koch's distinction: she says the causal distinctions become useful when it is a question of grounding human responsibility EITHER against the determinism attributed to the Stoics (the position attributed to Carneades) OR inside the doctrine that everything happens by fate (the position Chrysippus defends). Chrysippus grounds responsibility within fate; 'defending human responsibility against determinism' is Carneades' side. 'Auxiliary and proximate' is correct (pp. 99-100, l. 569-584: 'causes auxiliaires et prochaines (adiuvantes et proximae)'). Section I runs pp. 91-103.

scholarly_argument_l_hr_gnostic_determin.description: Löhr studies the 'hereseological cliché' of Gnostic determinism as it appears in Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria and Origen: a distinct heresiological tradition 'inaugurated/created by Irenaeus, developed by Clement and perfected by Origen'. He explicitly does not address whether the charge is a just description of any particular Gnostic source; he only argues, on a 'sceptical methodological approach', that before assessing the justice of the charge one must become aware of the heresiological attitude that generated it.

evidence.quote: Although we do not address ourselves to the extremely complicated question whether the charge of Gnostic determinism is a just description of the theological attitude of one particular Gnostic source or another, we assume that recent research on this question justifies our rather sceptical methodological approach
Our observations suggest that the cliché of Gnostic determinism is part of a distinct hereseological tradition that was inaugurated/created by Irenaeus, developed by Clement and perfected by Origen.

scholarly_argument_l_hr_gnostic_determin.finding: The quote_verbatim is in the file (ll. 22-27, p. 381) and the second sentence of the description is faithful. But the clause 'rather than being an accurate description of actual Gnostic theological positions' asserts what Löhr explicitly refuses to decide: he brackets 'the extremely complicated question whether the charge of Gnostic determinism is a just description' and only adopts a 'sceptical methodological approach'. His own thesis is genealogical: the cliché was 'inaugurated/created by Irenaeus, developed by Clement and perfected by Origen' (p. 386).

scholarly_argument_l_hr_irenaeus_s_anti_.description: Löhr reads Irenaeus' critique of Valentinian eschatology (haer. II,29) as 'the Christian version' of the 'lazy argument' with which the sceptical Academy had refuted Stoic determinism, and haer. IV,37,2 as a second 'philosophical argument against Stoic determinism': the completely determined cannot be praised or blamed. This second argument 'goes back at least as far as Aristotle', was 'probably' used by the Sceptic Academy, and was widely used in the 2nd century by Alkinoos, Alexander of Aphrodisias and Justin. Yet Irenaeus 'nowhere directly compares Valentinian determinism with Stoic determinism'.

evidence.quote: For example already the sceptical Platonic Academy refuted with the same argument (the so called […] the 'lazy argument') the determinism of the Stoics.

This argument goes back at least as far as Aristotle; it was probably used by the Sceptic Academy against the Stoics; it was widely used in the 2nd century by philosophers as, for example, Alkinoos or Alexander of Aphrodisias or theologians like Justin Martyr.
But although the bishop of Lyon refutes determinism with anti-Stoic arguments, he nowhere directly compares Valentinian determinism with Stoic determinism.

scholarly_argument_l_hr_irenaeus_s_anti_.finding: Both arguments are correctly located (lazy argument, haer. II,29, p. 382; praise/blame, haer. IV,37,2, p. 383) and the quote_verbatim matches ll. 99-108. Two slips: (a) Löhr says the praise/blame argument 'goes back at least as far as Aristotle', was 'probably' used by the Sceptic Academy and was widely used in the 2nd century (Alkinoos, Alexander, Justin) — the description transfers this diffusion to both arguments ('These were widespread'); (b) it drops Löhr's qualification that Irenaeus 'nowhere directly compares Valentinian determinism with Stoic determinism'. The Greek term in the description cannot be verified: the file's rendering is OCR-corrupt ([Greek-corrupt: '&py6q X6yoq']).

scholarly_argument_l_hr_clement_s_use_of.description: Löhr observes that Clement fights 'gnostic determinism' with philosophical concepts from several sources: the Aristotelian/Stoic concept of what is 'up to us' and the Stoic concept of 'the soul's faculty of assent', which 'guarantees its freedom and moral responsibility'. Taking up this Stoic term 'brings into play' Chrysippus' distinction between internal and external causes. Löhr judges the argument 'not a particularly strong and helpful' one: Basilides himself defined faith as an assent, and stressing assent 'was of no avail against a position that tried to argue with the nature of a person', since nature could be identified with the perfected faculty of rational assent.

evidence.quote: By taking up the Stoic term Clement brings into play another facet of the ancient philosophical debate about determinism: Chrysippus had defended the Stoic position against its Academic critics by distinguishing between internal and external, primary and secondary antecedent causes: The primary cause is always to be located inside man; it is precisely the soul's faculty of assent.
To be sure, Clement's employment of the Stoic term against Basilides and Valentinus was not a particularly strong and helpful argument.

scholarly_argument_l_hr_clement_s_use_of.finding: quote_verbatim matches ll. 167-181 (pp. 384-385). Three points: (a) 'paradoxically' is not Löhr's; he says 'it is interesting to observe'. (b) 'drawing on Chrysippus's distinction' overstates: Löhr says that by taking up the Stoic term Clement 'brings into play another facet' of the debate, then explains Chrysippus' distinction himself — he does not claim Clement drew on Chrysippus. (c) The two Greek terms in the description cannot be verified from the file: the Greek is dropped at ll. 154, 156, 161, 167 and OCR-corrupt at l. 171 ([Greek-corrupt: auYxaT&6Eavs]); Löhr's English is 'the soul's faculty of assent'. The assessment of weakness (Basilides' own use; nature = perfected faculty of assent) is faithful.

scholarly_argument_l_hr_origen_s_expansi.description: Löhr: Origen takes up Gnostic determinism 'at precisely that point where Clement had left it' — where Clement amalgamated Basilides and the Valentinians as teaching salvation by nature, Origen adds Marcion, so that the trio Valentinus/Basilides/Marcion recurs 'time and again'. In De principiis Origen develops Clement's suggestion of defending freedom by stressing 'the soul's faculty of moral choice or assent', against two extremes (freedom only without external influence; blame on inborn character). He 'does not leave the problem there': the souls' present differences stem from 'different moral choices in their previous existence'.

evidence.quote: Origen seems to take up the problem of Gnostic determinism at precisely that point where Clement had left it. Whereas Clement had made an amalgam of Basilides and the Valentinian position by asserting that both claimed that some are saved by nature, Origen adds the third great heretic of the 2nd century, Marcion.

But - as it is well known - Origen does not leave the problem there. […] Origen speculates about the possibility that the souls themselves are responsible for the differences in their present condition. These differences are not due to different natures, but they are accounted for by different moral choices in their previous existence.

scholarly_argument_l_hr_origen_s_expansi.finding: quote_verbatim matches ll. 182-197 (p. 385). But 'took up Clement's work at its weakest point' misreads 'at precisely that point where Clement had left it', which Löhr immediately glosses as the amalgam Basilides/Valentinians to which Origen adds Marcion — not a judgement about weakness. The description also omits Löhr's further step: Origen 'does not leave the problem there' and speculates that souls are responsible, through choices in a previous existence, for their present differences (p. 385).

scholarly_argument_mansfeld_aristotle_on.description: Mansfeld reports Frede's chapter 'Aristotle on Choice without a Will': Aristotle has no concept of will but one of 'willing'; prohairesis is choosing as a special 'form of willing', 'not between alternatives' but electing to do something; akrasia is 'misleadingly' rendered 'weakness of will' since no decision or choice occurs. Mansfeld adds a conclusion Frede does not draw (the bipartite soul precludes a single, free will) and objects that Aristotle's account of animal self-movement in De motu shows 'some simple form of will'.

evidence.quote: and not only argues that Aristotle does not have a concept of will although he has one of the closely related notion of 'willing', but also explains why he does not.

I think one may conclude from Frede's presentation of the evidence (though this is not what he says himself) that in his view the bipartition of the soul, each separate part being equipped with its own kind of desire, or willing, precludes there being room for a single will, let alone for a free one.
One can hardly fail to see commands of reason resulting in hekousioi kinēseis as representing some simple form of will.

scholarly_argument_mansfeld_aristotle_on.finding: The content (no will but 'willing'; prohairesis as a 'form of willing'; choosing 'not between alternatives'; akrasia 'misleadingly' rendered weakness of will because no decision occurs) is Mansfeld's epitome of Frede's chapter (p. 354). But 'Endorses' is wrong: Mansfeld reports, then draws a conclusion Frede does not state himself, and objects that Aristotle's analysis of animal self-movement (De motu) shows 'some simple form of will' (p. 355). The parenthetical 'boulēsis' is not in this paragraph (Mansfeld writes 'willing', with a note explaining the choice).

scholarly_argument_skarsaune_divine_fore.description: Skarsaune: the Christological testimonies of the 'kerygma' source 'express a Christology which focuses on Christ as the one who fulfils OT Messianic prophecies', with the two-parousias pattern safeguarding complete fulfilment (humility prophecies in the first coming, glory prophecies in the second). Justin exploits above all 'the simple correspondence between prediction and fulfillment', the 'formal proof-from-prophecy aspect'. Where 1 Apol 43f is discussed, Skarsaune notes Justin's assertion that prophetic foreknowledge 'in no way means that human choice and responsibility are annulled'.

evidence.quote: Justin exploits with most success the two parousias pattern, and the simple correspondence between prediction and fulfillment posited in the «kerygma. source, i.e. its formal proof-from-prophecy aspect, but he does not seem fully turned to the deeper concerns of this Christology.
evidence.citation: [The proof from prophecy _ a study in Justin Martyr's -- by Oskar Skarsaune -- .md:22160-22164] (Skarsaune 1987, p. 430)

evidence.quote: Let us now turn to the excursus in 1.Apol 43f.Justin here asserts that the phenomenon of prophetic foreknowledge in no way means that human choice and responsibility are annulled.
evidence.citation: [The proof from prophecy _ a study in Justin Martyr's -- by Oskar Skarsaune -- .md:9106-9108] (Skarsaune 1987, p. 160)

scholarly_argument_skarsaune_divine_fore.finding: quote_verbatim is verbatim at ll. 22073-22079 (printed p. 428, folio confirmed in the PDF). But the description's 'through divine foreknowledge and predetermined plan', 'not as philosophical free will arguments', 'evidence of divine design' are not Skarsaune's vocabulary or claims. His point about the kerygma source is the 'simple correspondence between prediction and fulfillment', the 'formal proof-from-prophecy aspect' (p. 430). Where he does touch foreknowledge (1 Apol 43f, p. 160) he records Justin's assertion that prophetic foreknowledge 'in no way means that human choice and responsibility are annulled' — the opposite of the antithesis the description builds. The page_range field holds md line offsets, not printed pages.

scholarly_argument_skarsaune_free_will_i.description: Skarsaune's study of Justin's proof-text tradition contains no thematic treatment of free will, determinism or moral responsibility. He registers the topic only in passing: 1 Apol 43f is an excursus 'on the compatibility of divine foreknowledge and human freedom of choice' (p. 160); Dial 102:3f an 'excursus on free will' (p. 221); 1 Apol 61:9f speaks of becoming children 'of free choice and knowledge' (p. 232); and the recapitulation passage Dial 88:4f/124 is quoted on men 'born in freedom of choice and with authority over themselves' (p. 392).

evidence.quote: 1.Apol39-45 (with two excurses: 1.Apol43f on the compatibility of divine foreknowledge and human freedom of choice; and 1.Apol46 on the responsibility of those living before Christ)

scholarly_argument_acosta_l_pez_de_mesa_.description: Acosta López de Mesa reports Frede: the Stoic notion of freedom, established by Chrysippus as exousia autopragias ('the ability to act one's own'), and the notion of will (an 'ability of the mind or of reason to make choices') are first combined into a free will by Epictetus. She accepts this reading of the Stoics but argues that their 'moral intellectualism' cannot genuinely explain choosing evil: since there are no irrational desires in adults and all impressions are rational, 'we always chose the good even if we mistake it by evil and evil is a mere accident caused by our ignorance of the real good'.

evidence.quote: Next, he shows that the notion of freedom came about ‚by analogy to the political notion of freedom‛ (10) that is finally established by Chrisyppus with his notion of exousia autopragias and is defined as ‚a matter of having the ability to act one’s own, to act at one’s own discretion, to act on one’s own account, to act independently‛ (66).

evidence.quote: However, Frede maintains that Chrysippus did not have a notion of the will and that the notion of a free will comes actually from Epictetus. According to the scholar, once we have our two ingredients, will and freedom, we have encountered the recipe for the free will and this is Epictetus’s achievement.
evidence.citation: [Plotinus Aristotle And TheOriginOfTheFreeWill-4213557.md:129-137] (Acosta López de Mesa 2012, pp. 34-35)

evidence.quote: It is not my goal to contradict this particular interpretation of the Stoics, which seems very plausible to me.

scholarly_argument_acosta_l_pez_de_mesa_.finding: quote_verbatim verbatim at ll. 150-155 (p. 35). The limitation claim is faithful, and 'all human impressions are rational' / 'no irrational desires in adults' are her report of Frede (pp. 34, 36). But the parenthesis misplaces the term: in her account exousia autopragias is Chrysippus' notion of freedom ('finally established by Chrisyppus'), while the free will arises with Epictetus once will and freedom are combined — the description makes exousia autopragias Epictetus' combination. She also says she does not contest Frede's reading of the Stoics (p. 36).

scholarly_argument_acosta_l_pez_de_mesa_.description: Acosta López de Mesa uses Plotinus as the 'exemplar' with which to show the limits of a 'purely rational will': he is 'also follower of this moral intellectualist tradition founded by Socrates and strengthened by the Stoics'. Since for him authentic freedom is self-determination in Intellect and evil is involuntary, 'the complexity of freedom is totally lost'; his philosophy 'is a philosophy suited for the One, not for human beings'. Plotinus thus illustrates the limitation, not a broader alternative — that alternative she finds in Aristotle.

evidence.quote: Thus, in order to show my own perception of the limits of the Stoic point of view on a purely rational will, I shall analyze Plotinus as exemplar.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_divine_elec.description: Dettwiler on Eph 1,4-6: the verses stress the election of the addressees 'dès avant la création' by the God of Jesus Christ; the language of election or 'prédestination' (v. 5), 'précédant tout agir humain', expresses 'l'idée d'une pure gratuité du choix de Dieu'. Vv. 7-10 then move from God's eternal project to its realisation in the historical action in Christ. Dettwiler says nothing about determinism.

evidence.quote: Les v. 4-6 soulignent l'élection des destinataires, dès avant la création, par le Dieu de Jésus Christ. Le langage de l'élection ou de la « prédestination » (v. 5), précédant tout agir humain, exprime l'idée d'une pure gratuité du choix de Dieu.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_divine_elec.finding: The sentence on election/'prédestination' expressing 'une pure gratuité du choix de Dieu' is verbatim (ll. 202-207), but it lies on printed p. 850, not 849 (PDF folio at page foot; agentic_search map_conf 0.90). More seriously, 'this is not deterministic in the philosophical sense' has no basis in Dettwiler, who never raises philosophical determinism; the node imports the thesis's frame into the commentary.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_human_moral.description: Dettwiler: Ephesians insists on an 'éthique du contraste' (4,17-5,20), stressing the necessary distance of the Pauline communities from the surrounding world and warning against excessive acculturation. This ethic is grounded in, not opposed to, prior divine action: it is 'fondée sur une expérience religieuse préalable dont elle ne saurait être dissociée', an 'éthique de la reconnaissance', following the Pauline indicative/imperative scheme (5,8); daily community life is 'le lieu de vérification de la nouvelle existence reçue par le Christ'. The instructions appeal to each member's responsibility and discernment (5,10.17).

evidence.quote: En fait, Ep insiste beaucoup sur une éthique du contraste (voir notamment 4,17-5,20]: elle accentue la nécessaire prise de distance des communautés pauliniennes à l'égard du monde ambiant
Le schéma paulinien classique de la relation entre« indicatif »et« impératif» se retrouve en 5,8
La vie quotidienne concrète de la communauté est le lieu de vérification de la nouvelle existence reçue par le Christ.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_human_moral.finding: 'Éthique du contraste' and 'nécessaire prise de distance' are verbatim (ll. 91-94, p. 847; developed pp. 861-862). But 'despite the prior divine initiative' inverts Dettwiler's relation: the ethic is 'fondée sur une expérience religieuse préalable dont elle ne saurait être dissociée' (p. 861), an 'éthique de la reconnaissance' (p. 854), structured by the Pauline indicative/imperative scheme (p. 862). Divine action grounds the ethical call; it is not its obstacle.

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_theological.description: Dettwiler: Eph 2,1-10 recalls to the addressees 'le contraste saisissant' between their past, marked by death, and their radically new present life in Christ. The former life was under the grip of death: they bore 'l'entière responsabilité' for their sins, yet it was 'une vie tragique, aliénée par les puissances démoniaques surnaturelles'. The accent falls on God as 'acteur déterminant', whose action is unconditional and creative love; the transfer from death to life is 'un acte de résurrection spirituelle' and a displacement 'dans les cieux', away from the demonic sphere.

evidence.quote: D'abord, l'auteur rappelle aux destinataires le contraste saisissant entre leur passé, marqué par la mort, et leur vie présente en Christ, radicalement nouvelle (2,1-10].

scholarly_argument_dettwiler_theological.finding: The 'contraste saisissant' between a past 'marqué par la mort' and 'leur vie présente en Christ, radicalement nouvelle' is verbatim (ll. 108-110, p. 847) and developed at p. 853, where God is 'acteur déterminant' and the transfer is 'un acte de résurrection spirituelle'. But 'rather than gradual moral improvement' is an antithesis Dettwiler never draws; he instead stresses that the addressees bore 'l'entière responsabilité' of their former sins while living a life 'aliénée par les puissances démoniaques'. Page 847 is correct for the introduction; the commentary proper is p. 853.

scholarly_argument_engberg_pedersen_paul.description: Engberg-Pedersen argues that Paul understood the pneuma 'as a through and through material, bodily phenomenon', as in Stoicism, where 'a material, bodily notion of pneuma' is central. His basic philosophical reference point was 'materialistic and monistic Stoicism' rather than the 'immaterialistic and dualistic Platonism' that had the upper hand in Philo; a 'Middle Platonic, immaterial understanding does not fit the facts', nor should the pneuma be read in exclusively 'apocalyptic' terms that dispense with the question of its ontological character.

evidence.quote: We shall ﬁnd that Paul understood the pneuma as a through and through material, bodily phenomenon.

evidence.quote: But we shall see that his basic, philosophical reference point was materialistic and monistic Stoicism—which indeed was importantly present in the two other writers, too—rather than immaterialistic and dualistic Platonism, which in Philo’s case, at least, had the upper hand.

scholarly_argument_engberg_pedersen_paul.description: Building on Paul Beyond the Judaism/Hellenism Divide (2001), Engberg-Pedersen holds that Paul's world-view 'is certainly a Jewish, apocalyptic one', but that 'parts of it are also spelled out by Paul in terms of Greco-Roman philosophical cosmology, in particular that of Stoicism'. In 1 Corinthians 15 Paul argues 'in a manner that should be called distinctly philosophical' (Stoic cosmology, Aristotelian physics, ekpyrōsis) while also drawing on Philo-type wisdom speculation and 'apocalyptic' imagery; between these 'thought worlds' there was 'no friction at all' — 'a frictionless fusion'.

The 'beyond the divide' framing is the author's (his 2001 volume, cited in the Preface). But 'his apocalyptic Jewish framework being expressible in Stoic philosophical terms' generalises what he states with care: the world-view 'is certainly a Jewish, apocalyptic one' of which 'parts ... are also spelled out' in Stoic cosmological terms; and at p. 37 the Stoic input sits alongside Philo-type wisdom speculation and 'apocalyptic' imagery in a 'frictionless fusion'.

scholarly_argument_king_augustine_s_earl.description: King: Augustine had no formal philosophical training and, distrusting sectarianism, pursued philosophy 'as a syncretistic amateur'. His initial knowledge came from the authors of his rhetorical education, 'Cicero and Seneca above all, in an eclectic mix heavily influenced by Stoic doctrines'. Most of these he knew 'in their non-technical popular forms' (unity of the virtues, rule of reason over the emotions, virtue as happiness, strength of character); only occasionally does he show more technical knowledge, e.g. the mind accepting or rejecting impressions in sensory experience (lib. arb. 3.25), which he handles correctly.

evidence.quote: Most of these doctrines Augustine knew in their non-technical popular forms: the unity of the virtues, the rule of reason over the emotions, the identification of virtue and happiness, strength of character as a defense against the vicissitudes of fortune. Yet he occasionally shows some knowledge of the more technical
Augustine speaks of the mind accepting or rejecting the impressions with which it is presented in the course of sensory experience – fundamental points of Stoic doctrine, which he handles correctly.

scholarly_argument_king_augustine_s_earl.finding: Located at pp. x-xi (in-file page headers 'Introduction / x', 'xi'; agentic_search refuses this AUDIT-FAIL file, map_conf 0.40). The description is accurate on Cicero/Seneca and the 'eclectic mix heavily influenced by Stoic doctrines', but it drops King's qualification that Augustine knew most of these doctrines 'in their non-technical popular forms' and only 'occasionally shows some knowledge of the more technical aspects', of which the accepting/rejecting of impressions (lib. arb. 3.25) is his one example.

scholarly_argument_labarri_re_anachronis.description: Labarrière opens by asking what Self/Soi can mean in ancient philosophy, recalling that 'Soi, employé substantivement' is an innovation of Locke's French translator Pierre Coste (1700), coined to render Self and to distinguish it from the Cartesian Moi by stressing what is 'réflexif' and 'subjectif' in it. He finds it astonishing that many recent publications, after the customary remark that nothing in Greek or Latin vocabulary 'corresponds' to our modern conceptuality, proceed 'comme si l'on parlait ... de realia'.

evidence.quote: Soi, employé substantivement, est une innovation du traducteur français de l’Essai sur l’entendement humain de Locke, Pierre Coste (1700), pour rendre Self et distinguer ainsi cette notion du Moi cartésien en insistant sur ce qu’il y aurait en elle de « réflexif » et de « subjectif » ?

nombre d’entre elles, après les remarques d’usage sur le fait que rien dans le vocabulaire grec, voire latin, ne « correspond » à notre moderne « conceptualité », embrayent comme si l’on parlait d’une façon ou d’une autre de realia

scholarly_argument_labarri_re_anachronis.finding: Both quotes are verbatim (ll. 55-58 and 60-63) and all on printed p. 7 (first page; the running head '8' opens l. 83). Two nuances lost: (a) the 'reflexive and subjective' connotations belong to Self/Soi ('insistant sur ce qu'il y aurait en elle de « réflexif » et de « subjectif »'), whereas the description's syntax attaches them to the Cartesian 'Moi'; (b) Labarrière proceeds by questions ('qu'est-ce à dire exactement ?') and attributes the 'no corresponding vocabulary' remark to the customary caveats of the publications themselves, with scare quotes on « correspond ».

scholarly_argument_labarri_re_to_eph_h_m.description: Labarrière's article asks what the fashionable category Self/Soi can mean for ancient philosophy — 'Soi' as a substantive being Pierre Coste's 1700 coinage to render Locke's Self, distinguished from the Cartesian Moi by its 'réflexif' and 'subjectif' overtones — and, after a selective survey of recent 'Self' literature, arrives at his own question: 'quoi du eph' hemin chez Aristote et Alexandre d'Aphrodise ?' The Coste remark concerns the word Soi, not the translation of to eph' hēmin.

evidence.quote: Self, ce terme est de plus en plus en usage en anglais et toujours aussi malaisé à traduire en français, surtout si l’on se tourne du côté des études en philosophie ancienne.
afin de parvenir à une question : quoi du eph’ hemin chez Aristote et Alexandre d’Aphrodise ? Je n’en dis pas plus à ce point.

scholarly_argument_labarri_re_to_eph_h_m.finding: The Coste quote is verbatim (ll. 55-58, p. 7), but the description conflates two things: the article's topic (to eph' hēmin in Aristotle and Alexander, against the vogue of 'Self' studies) and the remark on Coste, which concerns the coinage of 'Soi' to render Locke's Self — not 'the translation history' of to eph' hēmin. Labarrière makes no link between Coste's 'Soi' and eph' hēmin.

scholarly_argument_labarri_re_voluntary_.description: Labarrière recalls, with Vernant ('non sans raison'), that Aristotle's analyses of hekousion/akousion in EN III 'avaient aussi et peut-être surtout une portée juridique': what is at stake is the imputability of fault, and Aristotle himself says the definition is useful to legislators. Yet one must not forget 'le cadre plus large dans lequel elles s'inscrivent : l'arete, « vertu » ou « excellence ». Soit celui de l'acte' — knowing how to behave in each situation, which cannot result from mechanical application of rules. The section heading keeps the question open: 'Ébauches de la volonté dans EN, III ?'.

evidence.quote: « Jipé », comme nous l’appelions tous, commençait par rappeler, non sans raison, que les analyses d’Aristote sur ce que l’on appelle traditionnellement le « volontaire » et l’ « involontaire » (hekousion/akousion) avaient aussi et peut-être surtout une portée juridique.
il n’en faudrait pas pour autant oublier le cadre plus large dans lequel elles s’inscrivent : l’arete, « vertu » ou « excellence ». Soit celui de l’acte.

scholarly_argument_labarri_re_voluntary_.finding: quote_verbatim verbatim at ll. 222-226 (p. 10). But 'primarily juridical' hardens a hedged claim Labarrière attributes to Vernant ('non sans raison'): the analyses 'avaient aussi et peut-être surtout une portée juridique'. The section title is a question ('Ébauches de la volonté dans EN, III ?'); 'not reduced to modern concepts of will' is the node's inference. 'praxis' is not Labarrière's term here — he writes 'Soit celui de l'acte' (the Greek praxeis appears only inside the Bodéüs translation he quotes).

scholarly_argument_michon_akrasia_weakne.description: Michon recalls Davidson's reproach that Thomas confined incontinence to a face-off of reason and passion without recourse to the notion of will (p. 177). Against Davidson he notes that Thomas did introduce the will (voluntarium est a voluntate; the incontinent act is voluntary and even chosen, though eligens rather than ex electione). But this introduction adds no explanatory factor, since for Thomas the will follows the judgment of reason; the struggle still opposes reason to passion, and incontinence is a succession of judgments and therefore of wills (pp. 185-186).

evidence.quote: à homas, Davidson reproche de s’en être tenu, dans son analyse de l’incontinence, à un face-à-face de la raison et de la pas- sion, chacune procédant à son syllogisme pratique, et de n’avoir pas eu recours à la notion de volonté, qui aurait eu le mérite d’expliquer pourquoi une conclusion était préférée à l’autre.

contrairement à ce que disait Davidson, par exemple, homas a bien introduit le concept de volonté : toute action volontaire est due à la volonté (voluntarium est a voluntate), et l’acte incontinent est volontaire

Enin, l’introduction de la volonté n’ajoute pas de facteur explicatif supplémentaire, puisque homas rappelle qu’elle suit le jugement de la raison. L’incontinent choisit un acte, il le veut, et donc il le juge bon.

scholarly_argument_michon_akrasia_weakne.finding: Michon does say, against Davidson, that Thomas introduced the concept of will; but he immediately adds that this introduction adds no explanatory factor because for Thomas the will follows the judgment of reason, and that the struggle still opposes reason to passion. The node's clause 'Aquinas does employ the will in explaining why one conclusion is preferred to another' asserts exactly what Michon denies. Pages also wrong: Davidson's reproach is on p. 177 and Michon's reply on pp. 185-186, not 178-180.

scholarly_argument_michon_moral_responsi.description: Michon recalls Davidson's remark that Paul attributes his action to sin in him, which some read as hypocrisy and refusal of responsibility, and announces a reading of Paul that answers it (p. 177). Following Thomas: the ego is reason, distinct from the flesh which it should command though it may yield (p. 180). Under 'not I but sin' Thomas does not conclude that man loses free will, yet admits the sinner becomes sin's slave and loses 'la liberté de l'homme libre' (p. 181); in reading (i) the evil act is attributed principally to concupiscence, reason being instrumental (p. 182). Both readings express the doctrine of original sin and the fomes (p. 187).

scholarly_argument_schr_ter_reception_th.description: Schröter, Butticaz and Dettwiler (joint Introduction) ground the concept of 'reception' in the hermeneutical assumption that historical figures and incidents are accessible only through their remembering in texts, visual representations, rituals and the like: there is no direct, unmediated access to historical phenomena, which are always conveyed by their presentation in various media. This applies to Moses, David, Job, Jesus, Peter, James and Paul; even the 'historical Paul' is a reconstruction from the available evidence, and the volume does not aim to reconstruct him but to study his receptions.

scholarly_argument_van_kooten_free_will_.description: Van Kooten traces the development of Paul's anthropology against ancient Judaism and Graeco-Roman philosophy: man as the 'image of God' (Gen 1.26-27), transformed by 'assimilation to God' — the Platonic doctrine (Theaetetus 176b; Eudorus, Alcinous) whose nature is 'ethical' — and the 'trichotomic' anthropology of spirit, soul and body (1 Thess 5.23), a Greek philosophical reading of Gen 2.7 shared with Philo and Josephus. The two intertwine in the Corinthian letters as an anti-sophistic alternative to outward performance, and in Romans as a 'universalist anthropology' overcoming ethnic tensions, climaxing in the 'metamorphosis' of the mind (Rom 12.1-2). Free will appears only in 4 Ezra's theodicy.

scholarly_argument_van_kooten_free_will_.finding: The core of the description is right: the book is about the 'image of God', 'assimilation to God' (homoiōsis theōi) and the trichotomy of spirit, soul and body, and van Kooten does say the assimilation is 'ethical' in nature. Two losses. (1) 'analyzed in contexts where divine likeness and moral formation intersect with questions of human agency' is not van Kooten's framing: 'human agency' never occurs in the book (grep: 'agency' only for 'the agency of Moses'). His stated contexts are (a) the Corinthian sophistic movement — the two anthropologies 'become intertwined, with the sole purpose of offering an alternative to the outward, superficial, physiognomic anthropology of the sophists' [Kooten - 2008 - Paul's Anthropology in Context.md:444-447] — and (b) the ethnic tensions at Rome, answered by a 'universalist anthropology' climaxing in the metamorphosis of the mind in Rom 12.1-2 [Kooten - 2008 - Paul's Anthropology in Context.md:18815-18821, 18970-18986]. (2) The only free-will language in the book is confined to the 4 Ezra / Vision of Ezra theodicy discussion (pp. 14-15): the universalistic image of God 'is balanced with a particular understanding of human freedom and responsibility' [Kooten - 2008 - Paul's Anthropology in Context.md:1323-1324]; the description's 'rather than explicit free-will debates' is therefore correct but this locus should be named.
